findings.topic: Royal sacral authority and Louis XVI’s coronation
findings.source_grounded_note: The coronation juxtaposes divine kingship, ceremonial healing, sworn duties, court intrigue, and food unrest. The ceremony was customary rather than constitutive of kingship.

Conquest and dynastic inheritance produced enclaves, unequal provinces, generalities, parlement jurisdictions, and dioceses. Their mismatch created real jurisdictional conflict; geographical and historical functions qualify any picture of mere irrationality.

Map 1 depicts administrative, judicial, and fiscal divisions. Its caption is eligible descriptive text; map internals are not converted into an exhaustive place inventory under the graph-internals exclusion.

Roman and customary law, local weights and measures, the taille’s personal/land bases, six gabelle rates, exemptions, and internal customs barriers gave transactions and government markedly uneven conditions.

findings.topic: Paris basin, communications, and metropolitan integration
findings.source_grounded_note: Navigable rivers, roads, markets, commercial agriculture, literacy, and recognizable French distinguish this densely settled core; Rouen’s cotton industry draws on its labour supply.

Brittany combines distinctive language, provincial self-government, light taxes, good roads, and outward maritime ties; Vendée’s dispersed bocage settlements and weak ports favour isolation and subsistence. Young’s adverse impression of Brittany should remain attributed rather than erase those qualifications.

Fertility and navigable communications coexist with small cultivation and sharecropping. Bordeaux’s rapid commercial/population growth and suspicion of distant authority deserve access beyond an undifferentiated south-west heading.

findings.topic: Massif Central, Midi, and seasonal migration
findings.source_grounded_note: The Massif’s subsistence constraints, chestnuts, and labour migration contrast with Mediterranean vines/olives/mulberries; Dauphiné similarly exports seasonal workers while retaining memories of autonomy.

Camisard memory, anti-Protestant law, episcopal estates, and the Toulouse parlement qualify the reach of central toleration. Calas is introduced as a source of judicial notoriety, with fuller treatment elsewhere.

Provence’s representative and administrative arrangements coexist with a naval/penal port at Toulon and Marseilles’s Mediterranean/Levant trade and recovery after plague. Preserve the visitor attribution of alleged popular manners.
Lyons’s silk dependence and commercial identity differ from Burgundy’s transport-enabled industrial development, Le Creusot’s coke technology, and Lorraine’s charcoal metallurgy.

Franche Comté’s surviving serfdom and piety contrast with Alsace’s Lutheran toleration, Jewish population, German connections, Rhine trade, and advanced agriculture. Religious status must not be generalized nationally from Alsace.

Fragmented inheritance, tiny holdings, métayage, grain subsistence, manure scarcity, and fallow restrict yields. High-yield crops spread after crises; Flanders’s rotations and the Paris basin’s gros fermiers demonstrate market-responsive exceptions.

findings.topic: Rural burdens and varieties of tenure
findings.source_grounded_note: Tax, tithe, road corvée, and seigneurial obligations compete with producer resources. Distinguish lordship from ownership and cens/banalités/hunting rights from ordinary rents. Breton domaine congéable makes the later ownership-versus-feudalism classification consequential.

Uncertain harvests, volatile wine yields, forage failures, and continued rents disadvantage small cultivators while landlords prosper. Rural industry shares agricultural shocks; cotton exports and maritime commerce provide exceptions.

findings.topic: Colonial slavery and the two economies
findings.source_grounded_note: Slave-produced sugar/coffee and Atlantic re-exporting enrich ports, especially through Saint-Domingue, without broadly productive inland reinvestment. Coastal integration contrasts with interior stagnation and demographic pressure.

Insecure employment, real-wage decline, and family costs drive begging and migration. Towns attract migrants but mortality and inadequate work/relief undermine security. The author explains abandonment materially rather than accepting elite claims of moral collapse.

Mortmain restrictions, weak bequests, state debt measures, and inflation squeeze ecclesiastical relief. Philanthropic societies, masonic charity, dépôts de mendicité, and ateliers de charité mark experiments under pressure.

findings.topic: Village solidarity, common rights, and resistance
findings.source_grounded_note: Mixed livelihoods depend on commons, gleaning, grazing, and collective legal/extra-legal defence against enclosure, dues, and tithes. The curé can embody village solidarity while rich peasants contest his authority.

findings.topic: Rural social hierarchy and urban interdependence
findings.source_grounded_note: Coqs de village possess equipment, credit, jobs, and offices but solidarity with poorer neighbours is conditional. Markets, cottage industry, and migration link towns and countryside despite apparent separation.

findings.topic: Urban growth, poverty, and domestic service
findings.source_grounded_note: Port/capital growth differs from stagnant towns; most urban inhabitants remain poor. Servants receive material security but dependency, restricted family life, turnover, and proximity to wealth complicate their position.

Apprenticeship, compagnonnage travel, guild mastership, and workshop organization offer separate reader routes. Ménétra provides substantive biographical evidence. Access to mastership is not portrayed as uniformly closed despite familial advantage.

Exceptional factories, free trades, the attempted 1776 guild abolition, and the 1781 livret complicate the craft world. Inflation/unrest do not erase master–journeyman solidarities, especially against merchant control at Lyons.

findings.topic: Food prices, moral expectations, and Flour War
findings.source_grounded_note: Price controls, popular fair-price sales, hoarding fears, and women’s protest leadership are distinct mechanisms. Deregulation and poor harvests interacted in 1775; rioters commonly defended precarious livelihoods rather than having nothing to lose.

Bourgeois wealth, numbers, land/office ownership, consumption, education, theatres, books, and associations expand while poverty sharpens visible inequality. Do not reduce the bourgeoisie to only industrial entrepreneurs.
Security/prestige encourage conversion of trading profits into land, education, professions, and inheritable offices. Confessional exclusion qualifies the pattern for Protestants and Jews.
Robespierre’s legal and literary life in Arras and Barnave’s remembered Grenoble theatre humiliation give substantive person-specific routes into professional identity and relations with nobility.

findings.topic: Ennoblement, privilege, and the permeability of orders
findings.source_grounded_note: Office purchase and King’s Secretaries enable entry; privilege extends beyond nobles. Taille exemption has geographic exceptions, newer direct taxes include nobles, and dérogeance concerns retail trade with important loopholes.

findings.topic: Ségur Ordinance and the poor nobility
findings.source_grounded_note: The ordinance targeted rich recent entrants and supported poor hereditary nobles, though its public appearance suggested broad bourgeois exclusion. Courtiers still benefited, and experienced lower-rank officers were obstructed. Distinguish intention, reception, and effects.

The ruling group is a wealthy elite, with many poor nobles excluded. Commercial wealth continually replenishes noble wealth; rural gentry’s status, dues, and army aspirations distinguish them from court/urban wealth.

findings.topic: Debates on noble vocation and military education
findings.source_grounded_note: Coyer favours commerce; d’Arc proposes professional military monopoly and merit. Military schools, including Bonaparte’s Brienne, answer the livelihood and competence problem.

findings.topic: Army reform, recruitment, and social distance
findings.source_grounded_note: Prussian models shape disputed reforms. Volunteer regulars, foreign regiments, unequal militia conscription, regional concentration, and officers’ distance explain an army weakly integrated with much of society.

Red/blue officer recruitment, lack of purchase, and the classes reserve system differ from the army. Naval expansion helps secure American independence but its cost and Cherbourg works contribute to insolvency.

findings.topic: Clergy’s corporate status, assets, and finance
findings.source_grounded_note: Clergy’s spiritual function legitimates privileges; regular/secular composition, employment, property, tithes, Assembly, General Agency, free gift, and loans are separately useful routes. Exemption does not mean no contribution.

Concordat appointments, benefice patronage, noble family strategies, and Talleyrand’s career explain hierarchy and political skills. Parish clergy shoulder disproportionate taxes while wealthy chapters/regulars dominate governance.

findings.topic: Religious reform and revolt of the curés
findings.source_grounded_note: Jesuit expulsion demonstrates vulnerability; Brienne’s Commission of Regulars closes smaller houses. Portion congrue, tithe impropriation, blocked promotion, and exclusion fuel parish protest, suppressed without solving its causes.

findings.topic: Church power, toleration, and public order
findings.source_grounded_note: Worship monopoly, education, welfare, censorship, and announcements underpin political authority amid weak policing. Alsace remains an explicit exception to general Protestant disabilities.
Maréchaussée and town watch are small beside the elaborate venal judicial establishment. Competing jurisdictions, delays, and costs resist reform without legal uniformity or compensation.

Registration, remonstrances, publicity, strikes, and lit de justice define a constitutional practice; finance increasingly dominates disputes. The 1766 royal assertion and 1771–74 rupture need chronological distinction.

Exile, replacement, anti-venality reform, and new courts are reversed after Louis XV’s death. Restoration cannot restore either parlementary credibility or trust that monarchy is law-bound; this double loss is a central causal claim.

findings.topic: Robe elite, administrative careers, and kinship
findings.source_grounded_note: Masters of Requests and intendancies connect courts to ministerial government; kinship and shared social worlds temper conflict and explain the hostility to Maupeou’s outsiders.
Tax farming, venal financial offices, advances, loans, and public fund handling sustain government while private gains attract hostility. Paris’s customs wall symbolizes coercion and waste.

findings.topic: Versailles, court patronage, and political influence
findings.source_grounded_note: Court rank, costly display, royal rewards, and privileged access create dependency and influence. Polignac, Du Barry, Pompadour, Choiseul, and Maurepas illustrate concrete routes through favour to wealth and office.

The young king’s education, devotion, intentions, inexperience, and dependence on Maurepas qualify any simple incompetence label. Marie Antoinette’s upbringing and relations with the king are treated within the source’s strongly evaluative narrative.
